question: Rust around wheel nuts on a commercial vehicle most likely indicates what problem?
choice_a: The rim has been welded
choice_d: The brake drum is cracked
explanation: The manual states rust around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose and instructs drivers to check tightness, then re-check shortly after a tire has been changed.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Wheel and Rim Problems

question: According to the manual, what happens if one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring?
choice_a: Nothing, as long as the axle is secure
choice_b: The vehicle must be repainted before its next trip
choice_c: The vehicle will be placed "out of service"
choice_d: The tire warranty is voided
explanation: The manual specifically states that if one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, it will put the vehicle "out of service."
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Suspension System Defects

question: How much steering wheel play does the manual say can make a vehicle hard to steer?
choice_a: More than 5 degrees
choice_d: More than 15 degrees
explanation: The manual states that steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel) can make it hard to steer.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Steering System Defects

question: The CDL Vehicle Inspection Test recommends a method with how many steps?
choice_a: Five steps
choice_d: Seven steps
explanation: The manual describes a seven-step inspection method (Vehicle Overview, Check Engine Compartment, Start Engine/Inspect Cab, Turn Off Engine/Check Lights, Walk-around Inspection, Check Signal Lights, Start Engine and Check).
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method

question: When checking gauges after starting the engine, air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within how long?
choice_a: 1 minute
choice_d: 10 minutes
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes when checking gauges in Step 3 of the inspection.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Step 3 - Look at the Gauges

question: The manual says air pressure should build to a governor cut-out usually in what range?
explanation: The manual states the governor cut-out is usually around 120-140 psi, though drivers should know their specific vehicle's requirements.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Step 3 - Look at the Gauges

question: To test a hydraulic brake system for leaks, the manual instructs a driver to do what?
choice_a: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds
choice_b: Pump the brake pedal twice and hold for three seconds
choice_c: Pump the brake pedal five times and hold for ten seconds
choice_d: Apply firm pressure once and hold for five seconds without pumping
explanation: For hydraulic brakes, the manual says to pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Step 7 - Test for Hydraulic Leaks

question: Per the manual, drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo must inspect cargo securement how often?
choice_a: Only once, before departure
choice_d: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
explanation: The manual requires drivers to inspect cargo securement within the first 50 miles of a trip and every 150 miles or every three hours after that, whichever comes first.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.1 Safety Inspection

question: When backing a commercial vehicle, the manual recommends backing and turning toward which side whenever possible?
choice_a: Whichever side has more traffic
choice_d: It does not matter which side
explanation: The manual says to back toward the driver's side because you can see better; backing toward the right side is dangerous because you can't see as well.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: What does the manual recommend to keep a manual-transmission vehicle from rolling back when starting on a hill?
choice_a: Shift directly into the highest gear
choice_b: Release the clutch fully before applying any throttle
choice_c: Partly engage the clutch before releasing the brake, or use the parking brake/trailer brake hand valve
choice_d: Rev the engine to redline before releasing the brake
explanation: The manual advises partly engaging the clutch before taking your foot off the brake, applying the parking brake as needed, or using a trailer brake hand valve to prevent rolling back.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: How does the manual say a driver should hold the steering wheel?
choice_a: Firmly, with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
choice_b: Loosely with one hand near the top
choice_c: With both hands at the top of the wheel
choice_d: With the palms only, fingers extended
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to hold the wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides, so a curb or pothole cannot pull the wheel from their hands.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.2.2 Steering

question: What gear does the manual recommend using when backing a vehicle?
choice_a: The highest reverse gear available
choice_d: The lowest reverse gear, so you can correct steering errors and stop quickly
explanation: The manual says to always back as slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear, so you can more easily correct steering errors and stop quickly if necessary.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.2.4 Backing Safely - Back Slowly

question: According to the manual, what technique do most heavy vehicles with manual transmissions require to change gears?
choice_a: Float shifting only
choice_d: Clutchless shifting
explanation: The manual states that most heavy vehicles with manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: When should you downshift before descending a hill, according to the manual?
choice_a: Before starting down the hill, to a speed you can control without using the brakes hard
choice_b: Only after your speed has already built up on the grade
choice_c: Only if the brakes begin to fade
choice_d: Downshifting before a hill is unnecessary if the vehicle has a retarder
explanation: The manual says to slow down and shift down before starting down a hill, to a speed you can control without using the brakes hard, since hard braking can overheat brakes and cause loss of braking power.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.3.1 Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: The manual warns that retarders should be turned off under what condition?
choice_a: On dry pavement only
choice_b: When the road is wet, icy, or snow covered
choice_d: Only during heavy traffic
explanation: The manual cautions that when drive wheels have poor traction, a retarder may cause them to skid, so the retarder should be turned off whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.3.4 Retarders

question: Most good drivers, according to the manual, look ahead how many seconds?
choice_a: 5 to 8 seconds
choice_d: 12 to 15 seconds
explanation: The manual states most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, which is about one block at lower speeds and about a quarter mile at highway speeds.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

question: At highway speeds, looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead means looking about how far down the road, per the manual?
choice_a: About a quarter of a mile
choice_b: About an eighth of a mile
choice_d: About two city blocks
explanation: The manual says at highway speeds, 12 to 15 seconds ahead is about a quarter of a mile (about one block at lower speeds).
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.4.1 How Far Ahead to Look

question: The manual states mirror adjustment can only be checked accurately under what condition?
choice_a: While the vehicle is moving at highway speed
choice_d: Only in daylight
explanation: The manual states mirror adjustment should be checked prior to any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.4.2 Mirror Adjustment

question: According to the manual, how do objects appear in a convex ("fisheye") mirror compared to looking directly at them?
choice_a: The same size and distance
choice_b: Smaller and farther away than they really are
choice_c: Larger and closer than they really are
choice_d: Blurry but correctly sized
explanation: The manual explains that everything appears smaller in a convex mirror than it would look directly, and things also seem farther away than they really are.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.4.2 How to Use Mirrors

question: Per the manual's rules for turn signals, when should you cancel your turn signal?
choice_a: Immediately as you begin the turn
choice_c: Only if another driver honks at you
choice_d: After you have completed the turn
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to signal continuously through a turn and not forget to cancel the signal after the turn is complete.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Turns

question: Why does the manual say you should signal well before you turn?
choice_a: It is required at all speeds by federal law
choice_b: It is the best way to keep others from trying to pass you
choice_c: It automatically applies the trailer brakes
choice_d: It reduces fuel consumption
explanation: The manual states that signaling early is the best way to keep others from trying to pass you.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Turns

question: If you must stop on a road or shoulder, within how many minutes does the manual require you to put out emergency warning devices?
choice_a: 10 minutes
choice_d: 20 minutes
explanation: The manual states that if you must stop on a road or shoulder, you must put out your emergency warning devices within ten minutes.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence

question: On a one-way or divided highway, the manual says to place warning devices at what distances toward approaching traffic?
choice_a: 5 feet, 50 feet, and 100 feet
choice_d: 25 feet, 75 feet, and 150 feet
explanation: The manual specifies placing warning devices 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward approaching traffic when stopped on or by a one-way or divided highway.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.5.2 Communicating Your Presence, Figure 2.8

question: What three components make up total stopping distance, according to the manual?
choice_a: Reaction distance, swerve distance, and braking distance
choice_b: Perception distance, signal distance, and braking distance
choice_c: Alert distance, reaction distance, and skid distance
choice_d: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
explanation: The manual defines total stopping distance as perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 Stopping Distance

question: What is the average perception time for an alert driver, according to the manual?
choice_a: 1 second
choice_d: 3 seconds
explanation: The manual states the average perception time for an alert driver is 1 3/4 seconds, which accounts for 142 feet traveled at 55 mph.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 Perception Distance

question: At 55 mph, how many feet does the manual say reaction distance accounts for?
choice_a: 142 feet
choice_d: 216 feet
explanation: The manual states the average driver's reaction time of 3/4 second to 1 second accounts for 61 feet traveled at 55 mph.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 Reaction Distance

question: According to the manual, braking distance at 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes takes about how many feet?
choice_a: 61 feet
choice_d: 306 feet
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, braking distance can take about 216 feet.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 Braking Distance

question: The manual states that at 55 mph, total stopping distance is a minimum of how many feet?
choice_a: 419 feet
choice_d: 500 feet
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph, your vehicle will travel a minimum of 419 feet before coming to a complete stop.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 Total Stopping Distance

question: Per the manual, when you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, how much greater is the impact and braking distance?
choice_a: 4 times greater
choice_d: 16 times greater
explanation: The manual states that when you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, the impact is 4 times greater and the braking distance is also 4 times longer.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.1 The Effect of Speed on Stopping Distance

question: The manual recommends reducing speed by about how much on a wet road?
choice_a: One-tenth
choice_d: Three-quarters
explanation: The manual advises reducing speed by about one-third on a wet road (for example, slowing from 55 to about 35 mph).
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.6.2 Matching Speed to the Road Surface

question: What is the basic following-distance rule the manual gives for speeds below 40 mph?
choice_a: Two seconds regardless of vehicle length
choice_c: At least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
choice_d: One second for every 5 feet of vehicle length
explanation: The manual's rule is that you need at least one second for each 10 feet of vehicle length at speeds below 40 mph.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.7.1 Space Ahead - How Much Space?

question: Per the manual's rule, how many seconds of following distance should the driver of a 40-foot vehicle leave at speeds below 40 mph?
choice_a: 2 seconds
choice_d: 4 seconds
explanation: Using the rule of one second per 10 feet of length, a 40-foot vehicle should leave 4 seconds of following distance below 40 mph.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.7.1 Space Ahead - How Much Space?

question: In a 60-foot rig traveling below 40 mph, how many seconds of following distance does the manual say you need?
choice_a: 6 seconds
choice_d: 10 seconds
explanation: The manual states that in a 60-foot rig you'll need 6 seconds of following distance at speeds below 40 mph.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.7.1 Space Ahead - How Much Space?

question: If you are being tailgated, what does the manual say you should NOT do?
choice_a: Increase your following distance
choice_d: Signal early before slowing or turning
explanation: The manual says don't speed up if you are being tailgated: it's safer to be tailgated at a low speed than a high speed.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.7.2 Space Behind - Dealing with Tailgaters Safely

question: Why does the manual warn that clearing a bridge while loaded does not mean you can clear it while empty?
choice_a: Empty trucks are only narrower, not shorter
choice_b: Posted bridge heights change with the seasons
choice_c: An empty cargo van is higher than a loaded one
choice_d: Loaded vans have lower tire pressure than empty ones
explanation: The manual notes that the weight of a cargo van changes its height, and an empty van is higher than a loaded one.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.7.4 Space Overhead

question: How does the manual distinguish a "hazard" from an "emergency"?
choice_a: A hazard occurs only at night
choice_b: There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
choice_c: A hazard requires a written report, but an emergency does not
choice_d: A hazard is a possible danger; it becomes an emergency once you must react suddenly, such as when a car cuts in front of you
explanation: The manual's example shows a car signaling uncertainty is a hazard, but it becomes an emergency once the driver actually cuts in front of you and you must react suddenly.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.8.1 Importance of Seeing Hazards

question: What does the manual say the "slow moving vehicle" symbol looks like?
choice_a: A red triangle with an orange center
choice_b: A yellow diamond with a black exclamation point
choice_c: A blue circle with a white arrow
choice_d: An orange square with black stripes
explanation: The manual describes the slow moving vehicle symbol as a red triangle with an orange center, used to warn of vehicles like farm machinery.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards - Slow Drivers

question: The manual lists which of the following as an example of a vehicle with "blocked vision," a hazard clue?
choice_a: A motorcycle with a clean windshield
choice_b: Vans, loaded station wagons, and cars with the rear window blocked
choice_c: A taxi with a roof light on
choice_d: A bicycle with a rear reflector
explanation: The manual gives vans, loaded station wagons, and cars with the rear window blocked as examples of drivers who can't see others and are therefore hazards.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.8.3 Drivers Who Are Hazards - Blocked Vision

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 2 percent
choice_d: 23 percent
explanation: The manual cites the LTCCS finding that 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when CMV drivers were externally distracted (and 2 percent when internally distracted).
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: The manual cites research showing that talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would normally devote to safe driving?
choice_a: 20 percent
choice_d: 39 percent
explanation: The manual states that talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of 39% of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: Per the manual, the odds of a safety-critical event are how many times greater for CMV drivers who text while driving, compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 23.2 times
choice_d: 4 times
explanation: The manual states research shows the odds of a safety-critical event are 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers who text while driving.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.5 Texting

question: The manual says sending or receiving a text takes a driver's eyes off the road for an average of 4.6 seconds, which at 55 mph equals about how far, roughly the length of a football field?
choice_a: 142 feet
choice_d: 216 feet
explanation: The manual states that at 55 mph, 4.6 seconds of texting equals traveling 371 feet, or the length of an entire football field, without looking at the roadway.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.5 Texting

question: Per the manual, how long is a CDL disqualified after a second conviction (within 3 years) for texting or hand-held phone use while operating a CMV?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_d: 120 days
explanation: The manual states disqualification is 60 days for the second offense within 3 years of a hand-held mobile telephone or texting conviction.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.4-2.9.5 Cell/Mobile Phones and Texting

question: For three or more convictions within 3 years of the hand-held phone or texting prohibition, how long does the manual say a CDL is disqualified?
choice_a: 60 days
choice_d: 120 days
explanation: The manual states disqualification is 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years of a hand-held mobile telephone or texting conviction.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.9.4-2.9.5 Cell/Mobile Phones and Texting

question: How does the manual distinguish "road rage" from "aggressive driving"?
choice_a: Road rage involves the intent to do harm or physically assault another driver, while aggressive driving is operating selfishly or pushily without regard for others' safety
choice_b: They are the same term used interchangeably
choice_c: Road rage only happens on interstate highways
choice_d: Aggressive driving is a criminal offense, while road rage is not
explanation: The manual defines aggressive driving as operating selfishly, boldly, or pushily without regard for others' rights or safety, while road rage is operating with intent to do harm or physically assault a driver or vehicle.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.10.1 What Is It?

question: What does the manual say is the first and foremost thing to do when confronted by an aggressive driver?
choice_a: Speed up to get away from them
choice_b: Make every attempt to get out of their way
choice_c: Make eye contact to try to calm them down
choice_d: Pull over immediately and confront them
explanation: The manual states first and foremost, make every attempt to get out of an aggressive driver's way.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.10.3 What You Should Do When Confronted by an Aggressive Driver

question: According to the manual, getting how many hours of sleep or less triples your risk of a drowsy-driving crash?
choice_a: 8 hours
choice_d: 5 hours
explanation: The manual states that 6 hours of sleep or less triples your risk of a fatigue-related crash.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.11.2 Fatigue and Lack of Alertness - Are You At Risk?

question: The manual states you can see ahead about 250 feet with low beams, and about how far with high beams?
choice_a: 100 feet
explanation: The manual states that with low beams you can see ahead about 250 feet, and with high beams about 350-500 feet.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.11.4 Vehicle Factors - Headlights

question: Per the manual, you should dim your headlights within how many feet of an oncoming vehicle or a vehicle you are following?
choice_a: 500 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to dim their lights within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and when following another vehicle within 500 feet.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.11.5 Night Driving Procedures - Avoid Blinding Others

question: The manual states that working more than 60 hours a week increases fatigue-related crash risk by what percentage?
choice_a: 40 percent
choice_d: 60 percent
explanation: The manual states that working more than 60 hours a week increases your risk of a fatigue-related crash by 40%.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.11.2 Fatigue and Lack of Alertness - Are You At Risk?

question: What is the manual's best advice for driving in fog?
choice_a: Use high beams for maximum visibility
choice_b: Speed up to get through the fog quickly
choice_c: Don't drive in it; pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility improves
choice_d: Follow another vehicle's taillights closely to stay on the road
explanation: The manual states the best advice for driving in fog is don't; it's preferable to pull off the road into a rest area or truck stop until visibility is better.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.12 Driving in Fog

question: If you must drive in fog, what does the manual recommend regarding your lights?
choice_a: Use only your parking lights to avoid blinding others
choice_b: Turn off all lights to reduce glare
choice_d: Use low-beam headlights and fog lights, and turn on your 4-way flashers
explanation: The manual advises using low-beam headlights and fog lights for best visibility, and turning on 4-way flashers to give vehicles behind a better chance of noticing you.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.12 Driving in Fog

question: What minimum tread depth does the manual require on front tires, and on other tires?
choice_a: At least 6/32 inch on all tires
choice_b: At least 2/32 inch on front tires and at least 4/32 inch on other tires
choice_c: At least 4/32 inch on front tires and at least 2/32 inch on other tires
choice_d: At least 1/32 inch on all tires
explanation: The manual states you must have at least 4/32 inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires and at least 2/32 inch on other tires.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: According to the manual, what is one sign that ice has formed on the road ahead?
choice_a: A lack of spray from other vehicles
choice_b: Increased road noise from other vehicles
choice_d: Other vehicles driving faster than normal
explanation: The manual says a lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed on the road, and to also check mirrors and wiper blades for ice.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.2 Driving - Check for Ice

question: Why does the manual say not to use the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery winter surfaces?
choice_a: It wastes fuel unnecessarily
choice_b: It can cause the driving wheels to skid
choice_d: It is illegal in winter weather
explanation: The manual warns not to use the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery surfaces because they can cause the driving wheels to skid.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.2 Driving - Adjust Turning and Braking to Conditions

question: When crossing a deep puddle or flowing water, what braking technique does the manual recommend to keep mud, silt, sand, and water out of the brakes?
choice_a: Pump the brakes rapidly while crossing
choice_b: Avoid touching the brakes at all until fully across
choice_c: Slam the brakes on entry to the water
choice_d: Slow down, shift to a low gear, and gently apply the brakes to press the linings against the drums or discs
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to slow down, place the transmission in a low gear, and gently apply the brakes while crossing water to press the linings against the drums or discs and keep contaminants out.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.2 Driving - Wet Brakes

question: How does the manual say a driver should check that the cooling system has enough antifreeze before winter driving?
choice_a: By checking it with a special coolant tester
choice_d: By checking the tire pressure gauge
explanation: The manual states that the cooling system's antifreeze protection can be checked with a special coolant tester.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.1 Vehicle Checks - Coolant Level and Antifreeze Amount

question: How does the manual say you should adjust space to winter conditions?
choice_a: Drive alongside other vehicles for warmth
choice_b: Keep a longer following distance and avoid driving alongside other vehicles
choice_c: Shorten your following distance to reduce stopping distance
choice_d: Space adjustments are unnecessary if you have chains installed
explanation: The manual advises keeping a longer following distance in winter conditions and not driving alongside other vehicles.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.13.2 Driving - Adjust Space to Conditions

question: In very hot weather, the manual recommends inspecting tires how often?
choice_a: Every 500 miles
choice_c: Every two hours or every 100 miles
choice_d: Only at the start and end of a trip
explanation: The manual states to inspect the tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: What does the manual say to do if a tire is too hot to touch?
choice_a: Let air out to reduce the pressure
choice_b: Douse it with water to cool it
choice_c: Continue driving slowly until it cools
choice_d: Remain stopped until the tire cools off
explanation: The manual says if a tire is too hot to touch, remain stopped until the tire cools off; otherwise it may blow out or catch fire.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: Why does the manual warn never to remove the radiator cap until the cooling system has cooled?
choice_a: Steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns
choice_b: It will trigger the check engine light
choice_d: It causes the antifreeze to lose effectiveness
explanation: The manual warns that steam and boiling water can spray under pressure from a hot radiator and cause severe burns, so you should never remove the cap until the system has cooled.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Engine Coolant

question: What hazard does the manual describe as "bleeding tar" in hot weather?
choice_a: Tar rising to the pavement surface, creating spots that are very slippery
choice_b: Tar causing tires to overheat and blow out
choice_c: A chemical reaction that damages brake lines
choice_d: Tar fumes that can distract the driver
explanation: The manual explains that tar in the road pavement frequently rises to the surface in very hot weather, and spots where tar "bleeds" to the surface are very slippery.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.14.2 Driving - Watch for Bleeding Tar

question: How does the manual describe a "passive" railroad crossing?
choice_a: One equipped with flashing lights and bells
choice_c: One with no traffic control device, where the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely with the driver
choice_d: One found only in rural areas
explanation: The manual defines passive crossings as having no traffic control device, requiring the driver to recognize the crossing, search for a train, and decide if it is safe to cross.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.1 Types of Crossings

question: At a cross-buck sign with no stop line, how close or far must a vehicle required to stop position itself from the nearest rail of the nearest track?
choice_a: No closer than 5 feet, no farther than 25 feet
choice_b: No closer than 25 feet, no farther than 75 feet
choice_c: No closer than 10 feet, no farther than 40 feet
choice_d: No closer than 15 feet, no farther than 50 feet
explanation: The manual states vehicles required to stop at a cross-buck without a stop line must stop no closer than 15 feet and no more than 50 feet from the nearest rail of the nearest track.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Cross-buck Signs

question: How long does the manual say it takes a typical tractor-trailer unit to clear a single railroad track, and to clear a double track?
choice_a: At least 14 seconds for a single track and more than 15 seconds for a double track
choice_b: At least 5 seconds for a single track and 10 seconds for a double track
choice_c: At least 30 seconds for a single track and 45 seconds for a double track
choice_d: At least 20 seconds for a single track and 25 seconds for a double track
explanation: The manual states it takes a typical tractor-trailer unit at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds to clear a double track.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.5 Crossing the Tracks

question: What does the manual say about racing a train to a crossing?
choice_a: It is acceptable if the train appears far away
choice_b: Never attempt to race a train to a crossing, because it is extremely difficult to judge the train's speed
choice_c: It is only dangerous at night
choice_d: It is safe if you have a light load
explanation: The manual states you should never attempt to race a train to a crossing because it is extremely difficult to judge the speed of an approaching train.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.3 Driving Procedures - Never Race a Train to a Crossing

question: What does the manual instruct about shifting gears while crossing railroad tracks?
choice_a: Shift down for extra power to cross quickly
choice_b: Shift up once the tracks are cleared
choice_c: Do not shift gears while crossing railroad tracks
choice_d: Shift to neutral while crossing to save fuel
explanation: The manual explicitly instructs drivers not to shift gears while crossing railroad tracks.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.5 Crossing the Tracks

question: According to the manual, which vehicles are required to stop at the advance warning sign of a public railroad-highway crossing?
choice_a: Only vehicles over 26,000 pounds GVWR
choice_d: All passenger and hazmat-carrying vehicles
explanation: The manual states that all passenger and hazmat carrying vehicles are required to stop at the advance warning sign for a public railroad-highway crossing.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Advance Warning Signs

question: What factors does the manual say determine your selection of a "safe" speed on a downgrade?
choice_a: Total weight of vehicle and cargo, length of the grade, steepness of the grade, road conditions, and weather
choice_c: Only the number of gears in the transmission
choice_d: Only the time of day
explanation: The manual lists total weight of the vehicle and cargo, length of the grade, steepness of the grade, road conditions, and weather as the factors for selecting a safe downgrade speed.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.16.1 Select a "Safe" Speed

question: When should a driver shift into a low gear before descending a long, steep grade, according to the manual?
choice_a: Before starting down the grade, not after speed has already built up
choice_b: Halfway down the grade, once speed increases
choice_c: Only if the brakes begin to fade
choice_d: Shifting down is unnecessary with modern automatic transmissions
explanation: The manual warns not to try to downshift after your speed has already built up, because you may not be able to shift into a lower gear; shift down before starting down the grade.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.16.2 Select the Right Gear before Starting Down the Grade

question: How does the manual describe "brake fade"?
choice_a: A sudden loss of steering control
choice_b: Having to apply the brakes harder and harder to get the same stopping power
choice_c: The parking brake failing to hold on a hill
choice_d: Brakes locking up and causing a skid
explanation: The manual explains that brake fade means you have to apply the brakes harder and harder to get the same stopping power, caused by excessive heat from overuse.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.16.3 Brake Fading or Failure

question: How does the manual describe escape ramps built on steep mountain downgrades?
choice_a: Paved uphill lanes with rumble strips
choice_b: Water-filled channels that flood the wheels
choice_d: A long bed of loose, soft material designed to stop runaway vehicles safely, sometimes combined with an upgrade
explanation: The manual describes escape ramps as using a long bed of loose, soft material to slow a runaway vehicle, sometimes in combination with an upgrade.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.16.2 Select the Right Gear before Starting Down the Grade

question: What proper braking technique does the manual describe for controlling speed on a long, steep downgrade, using a 40 mph safe speed as an example?
choice_a: Apply the brakes hard enough to reduce speed from 40 to about 35 mph, then release, repeating as needed
choice_b: Hold the brakes down continuously from the top to the bottom of the grade
choice_c: Pump the brakes rapidly the entire way down
choice_d: Apply the parking brake instead of the service brakes
explanation: The manual describes applying the brakes hard enough to gradually reduce speed a few mph below your safe speed, then releasing them, and repeating this as needed down the grade.
source_note: SD CDL Manual, 2.16.4 Proper Braking Technique
